title: Taking Refuge in the Triple Treasures
speaker: Myoki Raizelah Bayen
summary: Myoki Raizelah Bayen's main teaching emphasizes the importance of cultivating a deep sense of unity and commitment within oneself by embracing the triple treasures of Soto Zen: the Buddha (our true nature), Dharma (the teachings that guide us), and Sangha (the community that supports us). This involves not just external practices, but also an inner transformation that allows us to live as vow, embodying the values of compassion, wisdom, and interconnectedness. By taking refuge in these three treasures, we can find peace, comfort, and connection with others, while also working to preserve and protect all beings through our daily lives.

One is from the perspective of the unified treasures, the second from the perspective of the manifested treasures, and the third from the perspective of the abiding treasures.
Let's take a closer look at each of these.
The first one, from the perspective of the unified treasures: the Buddha is alive in each one of us, and the Dharma reaches everywhere.
The Sangha includes the whole world.
There is nothing that exists outside of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
Rev Anderson writes:
*To take refuge in Buddha means to take refuge in what you really are.
It is simply you being you that is Buddha.*

*When you take refuge in Buddha, when you go back to being yourself fully, you begin to see how you are connected and dependent on everyone and how everyone depends on you.

When you take refuge in the Buddha, you begin to understand the teaching of interdependence, which is taking refuge in the Dharma.
And you honor your connection with other beings, which is taking refuge in the Sangha.*
He expresses quite clearly the unified three treasures.
From the perspective of the manifested three treasures, the Buddha treasure is the direct manifestation of Bodhi, the awakened mind, awakening.
Buddha was the first person to teach Bodhi.
This realization, though, has been passed through the generations, generations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The Dharma of the manifested treasure is, of course, the Buddhist teaching.
The teachings have also been passed to us through the generations of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
And the Sangha of the manifested treasure is our practice, together, here, with everyone, everywhere.
Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not limited by traditional concepts of time and space.
We are living Buddha's life right here, right now.
We're receiving the Dharma through all that life ever has and continues to teach us.
We're practicing with and for all beings throughout all the generations in the past and to come.
Life is refuge.
This is the manifested three treasures.
And from the perspective of the abiding three treasures, the spiritual meaning of the word abide means to preserve and to protect.

We're not practicing just for ourselves.
We're not practicing just to relieve our own suffering.

This is the path of the Bodhisattva.

Abiding in the three treasures is returning home, returning to who we really are, our true nature, our preconditioned nature, our original nature.
Knowing our [unclear: "Buddha head"] is to know that we are essentially love, and the Dharma teaches us to act with kindness and compassion.
The Sangha teaches us that we are all interconnected.
This is the abiding three treasures.
Maybe you've heard this story about our revered founder Dogen as he approached death.
Of all the practices in our tradition that he might focus on, it wasn't Zazen.
It was this practice of taking refuge.
He wrote in big black letters Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha on a long white piece of paper, and he hung this on a pillar in what was his death room.
He would summon his waning energy, get up from his sickbed and walk around this pillar chanting, Buddha, Dharma, Sangha.
This is our refuge, our place of peace, stillness, where Dogen turned, or returned, in his final days of life.
As Hana also pointed out this morning, we emphasize taking refuge when we sew a rakasu or an okesa: namu kie butsu with every stitch, namu kie butsu.
I take refuge in Buddha.
So many ways to say this.
I return home to myself.
I fly back to my true nature.
I take comfort in allowing myself to be myself.
I am comforted by being myself, like a child running to its parent.
I'm returning to my source.
I return to the source, the mystery from which all life emerges.
I take refuge in the boundless nature of all things.
